Now record the landscape. Taxonomy:

Root: "Time-aware retrieval and QA over temporally evolving text" 
Categories:
1. "Temporal-aware retrieval scoring" (parent: root)
   - "Soft temporal-semantic score fusion" — arxiv:2401.13222 (TempRALM), doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.295 (publication-year recency weighting)
   - "Hard version/validity-interval filtering" — arxiv:2605.23497 (RAG-kNN/ToC as-of date filter), doi:10.1080/08839514.2026.2626097 (TaxFlow temporal validity filtering)
2. "Temporal retrieval over structured knowledge" — doi:10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.394 (TimeR4)
3. "Temporal QA benchmarks" — doi:10.1145/3589335.3651895 (TIQ), arxiv:2605.23497 (statutory QA benchmark)
4. "Legal/regulatory QA systems (non-temporal or domain systems)" — doi:10.5220/0013751200004000, doi:10.1080/08839514.2026.2626097 (TaxFlow also here)
5. "Temporal-aware RAG for document domains" — doi:10.1109/bigdata66926.2025.11402566 (ESG, title-only)

Parent links: I'll use parent names.

idea_position: The idea sits at the intersection of "Soft temporal-semantic score fusion" and hard validity filtering, applied to legal/regulatory versioned corpora; it is essentially a domain transfer of TempRALM's soft fusion to amended statutes, positioned as retrieval-agnostic.

dominant_approaches: soft temporal score fusion added to semantic score (TempRALM); hard as-of-date/version filtering in legal RAG (Prior et al., TaxFlow); learned time-aware retrievers over TKGs (TimeR4); temporal relevance via metadata like publication year (health QA).

common_assumptions: temporal metadata (timestamps) available; temporal proximity/recency is the right proxy for relevance or validity; retrieval can be modified without retraining; queries carry or imply a date; end-to-end answer accuracy is the target.

common_datasets: TPQ-2019/2020, TIQ, PubMed health QA datasets, German statutory QA benchmark (312 pairs), Indian tax law corpus/benchmark, ESG documents, TKGQA datasets.

common_benchmarks: same.

common_metrics: Recall@k / MRR / nDCG; answer accuracy; F1; LLM-as-judge rubric; BLEU/ROUGE-L.

repeated_limitations (with ids):
- Recency preference harms historically anchored queries (recency bias) — arxiv:2401.13222, arxiv:2605.23497, doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.295.
- Temporal signal reduced to coarse proximity/year, ignoring validity intervals — arxiv:2401.13222, doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.295.
- Single-domain/single-jurisdiction evaluation, no public benchmark for overlapping revisions — arxiv:2605.23497, doi:10.1080/08839514.2026.2626097.
- Requires reliable timestamps on queries and documents — arxiv:2401.13222, arxiv:2605.23497.
- Soft vs hard constraint comparison absent — arxiv:2401.13222 (no hard baseline), arxiv:2605.23497 (no soft re-ranker).

underexplored_combinations:
- Soft elapsed-time fusion evaluated directly against hard validity-interval filtering on the same amended-statute corpus.
- Per-passage version timestamps at clause granularity with partially overlapping revisions.
- Temporal decay conditioned on query-date regime (historical vs current) rather than monotone recency.
- Retrieval-agnostic wrapper validated across multiple retriever families (sparse + dense) and multiple domains.
- Validity-interval-aware temporal score (piecewise/in-force indicator) instead of distance decay.

contradictions (with ids):
- arxiv:2605.23497 vs arxiv:2401.13222: hard constraint ("what is retrieved matters more than how") vs soft score fusion; Prior et al. report recency bias from retrieval/recency signals, TempRALM treats recency as a gain. Also Prior et al. say temporal validity should be a hard constraint, contradicting soft decay as a sufficient mechanism.
- doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.295 favors recent evidence unconditionally; arxiv:2605.23497 shows favoring recent passages harms historically anchored queries.

Let me record. Also record a new uncertainty? Maybe U006: whether a new benchmark is needed — already U003. I think no new uncertainty needed here; the synthesize step adds landscape. But instructions say record new questions throughout. I could add U006 about construct validity: whether overlapping-revision benchmark can be built without synthetic queries (Prior et al. used LLM-synthesized expert-validated questions). Hmm, that's a real one: the benchmark might be synthetic. Let me add U006 about benchmark construct validity / whether a real-world time-stamped QA set with overlapping revisions exists vs synthetic. Actually U003 already asks whether a benchmark already exists. A distinct question: whether synthetic LLM-generated time-sensitive queries (as in Prior et al.) are valid evidence for retrieval-ranking claims. That's an evaluation uncertainty. Let me add U006.

input.field_name: Time-aware retrieval and question answering over temporally evolving documents

categories.description: Retrieval and question answering when documents, facts or provisions change over time, so the correct answer depends on a time reference.
categories.name: Time-aware retrieval and QA (root)

categories.description: Approaches that modify how candidates are scored or selected using a time signal.
categories.name: Temporal-aware retrieval scoring

categories.description: Add a continuous temporal term (elapsed time, recency, publication year) to a semantic similarity score, without retraining or re-indexing.
categories.name: Soft temporal-semantic score fusion

categories.description: Extract an as-of date and restrict the retrieval space to document versions in force during that period, treating temporal validity as a hard constraint.
categories.name: Hard version / validity-interval filtering

categories.description: Retrievers fine-tuned with time-aware objectives over timestamped graph facts, with question rewriting and temporal reranking.
categories.name: Learned time-aware retrieval over structured temporal knowledge

categories.description: Datasets of time-sensitive questions with ground-truth answers and supporting evidence: multi-source implicit-time QA and time-sensitive statutory QA.
categories.name: Temporal QA benchmarks

categories.description: End-to-end assistants over statutes, tax law and legal corpora, some with temporal validity handling and some without an explicit temporal component.
categories.name: Domain-specific legal / regulatory RAG systems

categories.description: Time-sensitive QA over ESG and biomedical documents, where recency of evidence functions as a relevance signal.
categories.name: Temporal-aware RAG in non-legal document domains

input.idea_position: The idea sits in the "Soft temporal-semantic score fusion" sub-category, but transfers it to the legal/regulatory setting that is currently dominated by "Hard version / validity-interval filtering". Its distinctive framing is retrieval-agnostic soft re-ranking of overlapping document versions by elapsed time to the query date, positioned against hard in-force-date filtering as the baseline.
dominant_approaches: Add a temporal term to the semantic retrieval score (exponential/reciprocal time difference, normalized and summed), possibly masking future-dated passages (arxiv:2401.13222)
Extract an as-of date and hard-filter the retrieval corpus to the version valid at that date (arxiv:2605.23497, doi:10.1080/08839514.2026.2626097)
Fine-tune a time-aware retriever with contrastive learning and rerank by explicit temporal constraints (doi:10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.394)
Use publication year / recency as a document-quality re-weighting signal in open-domain QA (doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.295)
Construct time-sensitive benchmarks with LLM-generated, expert-validated questions whose fact date determines the correct version (arxiv:2605.23497)
common_assumptions: Usable timestamps exist for queries (or can be extracted) and for documents/versions
Temporal proximity or recency is an adequate proxy for temporal relevance or legal validity
Retrieval can be modified post-hoc without retraining the underlying model
Answer accuracy (often LLM-as-judge) is the primary success measure
Documents from different time points co-exist in one corpus, producing dense semantic overlap
common_datasets: German statutory QA benchmark, 312 expert-validated pairs (arxiv:2605.23497)
PubMed with three health QA datasets (doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.295)
Curated Indian tax statutes/gazettes plus a unified tax-law benchmark (doi:10.1080/08839514.2026.2626097)
Two unnamed temporal knowledge graph QA datasets (doi:10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.394)
common_metrics: LLM-as-a-judge rubric score validated against expert ratings

repeated_limitations.description: Recency-oriented temporal signals harm historically anchored queries: the same mechanism that fixes post-amendment staleness introduces recency bias when the applicable version is older.
Temporal signal is reduced to coarse proximity or publication year, ignoring explicit validity/effective-date intervals, so a temporally near version may still be legally inapplicable.
Evaluation is confined to a single jurisdiction, language or domain, and no shared public benchmark of overlapping regulatory revisions exists.
The approach presupposes reliable per-query and per-document timestamps; both are asserted or regex-extracted rather than stress-tested for noise and missingness.
Soft temporal scoring and hard validity filtering are never compared head-to-head on the same corpus and retriever: TempRALM lacks a hard-constraint baseline, and Prior et al. test no soft re-ranker.
Retrieval-agnosticism is claimed but only one retriever family is instantiated, so cross-retriever generalisation is unverified.

underexplored_combinations: A direct head-to-head comparison of soft elapsed-time score fusion versus hard validity-interval filtering on the same amended-statute corpus with the same retriever
Validity-interval-aware temporal scoring (in-force indicator or piecewise decay) instead of monotone distance decay, which would reconcile the soft/hard contradiction
Query-date-regime-conditioned temporal weighting that avoids recency bias on historically anchored queries
Retrieval-agnostic evaluation across multiple retriever families (BM25 plus several dense encoders) with and without re-indexing, on the same benchmark
Benchmarks with clause-level, partially overlapping successive revisions plus per-passage version timestamps, as opposed to snapshot QA pairs or knowledge-graph facts
Joint evaluation of retrieval-layer metrics (version-selection accuracy, Recall@k) and end-task answer accuracy in the legal temporal setting

contradictions.description: Hard constraint versus soft score: Prior et al. conclude that legal temporal validity must be enforced as a hard constraint and that the correct timeframe matters more than the retrieval method, whereas TempRALM's core contribution is a soft temporal score added to semantic similarity that improves accuracy without any validity constraint.

Recency as benefit versus recency as bias: Vladika and Matthes treat preferring more recent evidence as a gain (+10% macro F1), while Prior et al. and TempRALM's own design constraints show that preferring newer provisions is a failure mode for historically anchored questions.

Training-free score adjustment versus learned time-aware retrieval: the idea and TempRALM avoid retraining, whereas TimeR4 fine-tunes a contrastive time-aware retriever and reports large gains, leaving it open which is necessary when temporal constraints are complex.

input.description: The only retrieved resource with version-aware statutory questions (arxiv:2605.23497) uses LLM-synthesized questions, subsequently expert-validated; TIQ is fully automatically generated. A benchmark of overlapping regulatory revisions with time-stamped queries would likely also need to be synthesized. It is unclear whether synthetic time-sensitive queries support valid claims about retrieval-ranking behaviour on real amended corpora, or whether they risk encoding the generator's own recency assumptions.
input.question: Can a benchmark of overlapping regulatory revisions with time-stamped queries be built whose labels are valid evidence about real retrieval behaviour, given that existing temporal legal QA sets are LLM-synthesized (with expert validation) rather than drawn from real time-stamped user queries?
input.rationale: Construct validity of the planned benchmark is a precondition for any claim that a soft temporal score improves answer accuracy; if synthetic queries encode recency assumptions, the main result could be circular.

I recorded the research landscape: an 8-category taxonomy (root "Time-aware retrieval and QA", with soft temporal-semantic score fusion, hard version/validity-interval filtering, learned time-aware retrieval over temporal knowledge, temporal QA benchmarks, legal RAG systems, and non-legal temporal RAG), placing the idea in the soft-fusion sub-category applied to the legal domain currently dominated by hard filtering.

I also captured the dominant approaches, common assumptions/datasets/benchmarks/metrics, six repeated limitations with paper ids (notably the recency-bias trade-off shared by `arxiv:2401.13222`, `arxiv:2605.23497`, `doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-naacl.295`, and the missing head-to-head soft-vs-hard comparison), six underexplored combinations, and three explicit contradictions — hard validity constraint (`arxiv:2605.23497`) versus soft temporal fusion (`arxiv:2401.13222`), and recency as benefit versus recency as bias — plus new uncertainty U006 on the construct validity of synthetic time-stamped query sets.
